opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the most important questions, because a model can look great on standard short-range metrics and still be completely unusable for anything beyond a week or two.

For the first few days, we look at the usual things: RMSE, anomaly correlation, compared against ECMWF's operational system. But those metrics reward blurriness. If you're unsure, the safest bet under mean squared error is to predict the average, so a model can score well while gradually smoothing out every storm and front. That's a sign the model hasn't really learned the physics.

So for long rollouts we look at physical consistency. A big one is the energy spectrum. The atmosphere has a characteristic distribution of energy across spatial scales, and you can check whether the model preserves it over time. A lot of early models lost the small scales, and the field got smoother and smoother. Others went the other way: energy piled up at high frequencies, you'd get these grid-scale artifacts, and eventually the rollout blew up.

That was a key motivation for the spherical Fourier neural operator work. The Earth is a sphere, and treating it as a flat image with standard FFTs or convolutions creates artifacts at the poles and boundaries. Those small errors compound over hundreds of autoregressive steps. Working in a spherical harmonic basis respects the geometry, and we found we could roll out stably for a year or more of simulated time without the model diverging. That's something many earlier approaches couldn't do.

Beyond stability, we ask whether the long-run statistics are right. Does the model produce a sensible climatology? Do you get realistic seasonal cycles? Do you see phenomena like tropical cyclones forming with plausible frequencies and intensities? At that horizon you're no longer predicting the exact weather, since chaos makes that impossible. The question is whether you're sampling from the right distribution.

That leads to ensembles. For long horizons the honest answer is probabilistic, so we generate large ensembles cheaply, which is a big advantage of these models over traditional numerical weather prediction, and evaluate them with metrics like CRPS and spread-skill ratios. We want the uncertainty to be calibrated, not just the mean to be accurate.

The bigger philosophical point is that if these models are to be useful for subseasonal or climate applications, they have to learn the underlying dynamics, not memorize patterns from the training data. Long rollouts are really a stress test for that. If the physics isn't right, it shows up eventually, and usually dramatically.

r001.rationale: The response says long rollouts require physical consistency and that incorrect physics eventually causes dramatic failure; it also describes respecting spherical geometry as helping preserve stability.

r002.rationale: It contrasts flat-image approaches, which create compounding geometric artifacts, with spherical harmonics, which enabled stable rollouts for a year or more; it says many earlier approaches could not do this.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the things I'm most proud of with FourCastNet and the work that followed. When we started, the big worry everyone had about learned weather models was stability. You train a model to predict six hours ahead, and then you feed its own output back in as the next input, and you do that again and again. Any small error compounds. So the natural expectation was that these models would blow up, that after a few days you'd get unphysical fields, energy drifting off, that kind of thing.

What we found with FourCastNet was that we could run it out for weeks and it stayed stable, and actually quite realistic looking. Not accurate in the sense of matching the exact weather on day twenty, nobody can do that, the atmosphere is chaotic. But stable in the sense that the statistics looked like real weather. The energy spectra were right, the large-scale circulation patterns were right, you didn't see the model collapsing to some smeared-out mean or going off into some crazy regime.

And then with the spherical Fourier neural operator work, SFNO, we really pushed on this. The key insight there was respecting the geometry. The earth is a sphere, and if you treat it as a flat grid with periodic boundaries you get artifacts at the poles that build up over long rollouts. Once we built the operator directly on the sphere, using spherical harmonics, we could run the model out for a year, more than a year, of autoregressive steps, and it remained stable. That was a big deal because it opened up the possibility of using these models not just for medium-range forecasting but for seasonal and even climate-type studies.

In terms of how we actually assess it, there are a few things we look at. The first is just the basic skill metrics, RMSE and anomaly correlation against reanalysis data like ERA5, and we track how those degrade over lead time compared to numerical weather prediction. Then for the long rollouts, where you can't compare against the specific trajectory anymore, we look at the climatology. Does the mean state stay reasonable? Does the variability match? We look at the power spectra across spatial scales, because a common failure mode is that the model loses small-scale energy and everything gets blurry. And we look at things like the annual cycle, whether it correctly captures seasons as you integrate forward, since the model is partly conditioned on time of year.

I'd also say we're honest that this is still an open area. Long-term stability is necessary but not sufficient. A model can be stable and still have subtle biases that would matter for climate work. So the next frontier for us is really coupling, bringing in the ocean, bringing in physical constraints more directly, and doing proper ensemble evaluation to understand the uncertainty. But the fact that a purely learned model can sustain these rollouts at all, that was genuinely surprising to a lot of people in the field, and it's what convinced me this direction was going to be transformative.

r001.rationale: The response says long-term stability is necessary but not sufficient and names adding physical constraints as a next frontier; it does not say physical constraints are necessary to sustain long rollouts.

r002.rationale: It says spherical geometry helped SFNO remain stable for over a year and contrasts this with flat-grid pole artifacts, but does not explicitly claim longer rollouts than other weather models that disregard spherical geometry.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish stability from accuracy. A model can keep producing something that looks like weather for a very long time, but that doesn’t mean it’s predicting the actual weather correctly.

So you run it autoregressively—take its prediction, feed that back in, and repeat—and measure how errors grow with the forecast horizon. You also want to look beyond average error: Are the large-scale patterns reasonable? Is the variability maintained? Does the model drift toward an unrealistic state, or smooth away important extremes?

And because weather is chaotic, eventually you lose predictability of the specific trajectory. At that point, the question becomes whether the model preserves the right statistics. Those are different tests, and I’d want to see both before claiming that a model sustains very long rollouts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating rollout stability, error growth, and preserved statistics, but does not state that physical constraints are necessary.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison between Anandkumar’s models and models that disregard Earth’s spherical geometry.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is to test the model beyond the horizon it was trained on. You take its prediction, feed that back in as the next input, and keep going. Errors accumulate, so a model that looks very good on a single step can still become unstable over a long rollout.

We look at both forecast skill and whether the evolution remains physically reasonable. Does it preserve the large-scale circulation? Do the statistics drift? Does energy build up in ways that are unphysical? And we distinguish stability from predictability: a rollout can remain stable without accurately predicting the particular weather months into the future. At those longer horizons, the question becomes whether it captures the right statistics, rather than the exact trajectory.

r001.rationale: The response discusses checking physical reasonableness, but does not state that incorporating physical constraints is necessary for sustaining long rollouts.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison with other weather models or mention of Earth's spherical geometry.
